concept.name: Spinning top
concept.definition: A single candlestick with a small real body vertically centered between upper and lower shadows that are both noticeably longer than the body. Like the doji, it is read as indecision between buyers and sellers and is treated in technical analysis as a possible sign of trend exhaustion when it follows an extended move; it is a hypothesis requiring confirmation, not a predictive law.
concept.intuition: Both bulls and bears pushed price around during the period, but neither could keep it anywhere; the close near the open shows the tug-of-war ended in a draw.
concept.mechanics: Identified from OHLC data: the real body |close - open| is small relative to the total range (larger than a doji's near-zero body; a common convention allows up to roughly 5% of the range before calling it a doji instead), with meaningful shadows on both sides. The close may be above or below the open.
concept.failure_modes: Spinning tops are extremely common, so most occurrences are inconsequential, especially within ranges. Even after extended trends, many spinning tops are followed by continuation rather than reversal.
concept.misconceptions: A spinning top does not predict a reversal on its own; the following candle must confirm. It is also not the same as a doji: its body is small but visible.
concept.example: After a long advance, a stock opens at 80.00, trades between 78.50 and 81.50, and closes at 80.20. The spinning top hints that buyers are losing control; a strong down candle the next day would confirm a reversal reading.
